questions.q: In the ten-minute talk budget this lesson gives, which section gets the most time?
questions.explain: The suggested budget gives Result four of the ten minutes, more than Problem, Method, or What's next — a technical audience wants the actual numbers.

questions.q: What does this lesson mean by 'one claim per slide'?
options: Every slide should contain exactly one word
If a slide is making two points, it should be split into two slides
Each slide should repeat the thesis of the talk
questions.explain: The rule is that a slide making two points should become two slides, keeping each slide defensible on a single claim.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what is the first thing a technical audience looks for on a chart?
questions.explain: The lesson states a technical audience will look for the baseline before anything else on a chart, which is why axes and baselines must be labeled.

questions.q: If a technical audience member asks 'how many runs or seeds,' and the honest answer is one, what does this lesson recommend?
options: Avoid answering and change the subject
Claim there were more runs than there actually were
Say it was one, and say what you'd do with more time
Cancel the rest of the talk
questions.explain: The lesson's guidance is to answer honestly — say one if it's one — and describe what you'd do with more time, rather than overstating the evidence.

questions.q: This lesson says 'what would change your conclusion' is really a restatement of which earlier concept?
options: The minimal viable experiment from Lesson 3
The falsifiability test from Lesson 2, asked out loud
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly ties this question back to the falsifiability test introduced in Lesson 2 on picking a research question.
